nameStory: Common butterwort gets its name from the greasy, butter-like feel of its leaves, which are covered in tiny glands that produce a slippery coating. This slick surface isn't just for show – it's actually a clever trap that helps this little plant catch and digest tiny insects for extra nutrition.
description: Common butterwort is a small, low-growing carnivorous plant that forms rosettes of pale green, greasy-feeling leaves pressed close to the ground. The entire plant is only 2-6 inches tall, with delicate purple flowers that rise above the leaf cluster on thin stalks. Unlike the dramatic snap-traps of Venus flytraps, butterwort catches its prey with a much more subtle approach – tiny insects simply get stuck on the slippery leaf surfaces and are slowly digested.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-green leaves arranged in a flat rosette, each leaf feeling distinctly greasy or buttery to the touch due to tiny digestive glands covering the surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single violet-purple flowers with two lips and a white throat, sitting alone on thin 2-4 inch stalks that rise from the center of the leaf rosette

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, flat rosettes hugging the ground, rarely more than 3 inches across, often growing in small colonies

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel slick and oily when touched, often with tiny bits of debris or dead insects stuck to the surface

habitat: Found in wet, nutrient-poor environments like sphagnum bogs, wet rocky ledges, and seepy cliff faces throughout northern New England. Prefers calcium-rich soils and cool, moist conditions, often growing alongside other bog plants like sundews and pitcher plants in acidic wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Leaf rosettes emerge from winter dormancy, appearing fresh and bright green with their characteristic greasy texture becoming prominent.
seasonality.summer: Purple flowers bloom from June through August, rising on delicate stalks above the leaf rosettes. This is the best time to spot the plant when flowers make it more visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may begin to yellow slightly, but the rosettes remain visible and identifiable by their distinctive buttery feel.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to underground buds, becoming completely dormant and invisible until spring growth resumes.

funFact: This tiny plant is actually a meat-eater that can digest an entire gnat in just a few days using enzymes secreted from thousands of microscopic glands on its leaves – essentially turning each leaf into a living digestive surface!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with sundews, which also grow in bogs and catch insects, but sundews have obvious sparkly dewdrops on their leaves while butterwort leaves are simply greasy and slick with no visible droplets.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' butterwort, this plant is actually quite rare in New England and is considered a species of conservation concern in several states due to habitat loss and the destruction of bog ecosystems.
compareHints: Common butterwort is the only butterwort species found in New England, making identification straightforward once you recognize the genus. It's most similar to other small carnivorous bog plants like sundews and bladderworts in its family, but differs by having greasy rather than sticky-dewdrop leaves and lacking the tiny bladder traps of aquatic bladderworts.
